title: Full Syllabus Test
description: Topics: Algebra, Trigonometry, Functions, Limits, Continuity, Differentiation, Applications of Derivatives, Integration, Area, Differential Equations, Matrices, Determinants, Systems of Linear Equations · Questions: 30

questions.prompt: The number of real solutions of $\lvert x^{2}-3x+2\rvert=2\lvert x-1\rvert$ is
questions.explanation: Factor: $\lvert(x-1)(x-2)\rvert=2\lvert x-1\rvert$. If $x=1$, both sides vanish, so $x=1$ is a solution. If $x\neq 1$, cancel to get $\lvert x-2\rvert=2$, hence $x=0$ or $x=4$. All three values work, so there are $3$ real solutions.

questions.prompt: The solution set of $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-3x+2}\le 0$ is
questions.explanation:
$$
\dfrac{(x-2)(x-3)}{(x-1)(x-2)}\le 0,\qquad x\neq 1,\,2.
$$

For $x\neq 2$ this is $\dfrac{x-3}{x-1}\le 0$, whose solution is $1\le x\le 3$. Removing the undefined points $x=1$ and $x=2$ leaves $(1,2)\cup(2,3]$.

questions.prompt: The number of solutions of $\sin 3x=\sin 2x$ in the interval $(0,2\pi)$ is
questions.explanation:
$\sin A=\sin B$ gives $3x=n\pi+(-1)^{n}2x$. Even $n=2k$ yields $x=2k\pi$, none in $(0,2\pi)$. Odd $n=2k+1$ yields $x=(2k+1)\pi/5$. The values in $(0,2\pi)$ are

$$
\dfrac{\pi}{5},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{5},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{7\pi}{5},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{5},
$$

so there are $5$ solutions.

questions.prompt: If $\sin\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$, then $\cos^{12}\theta+3\cos^{10}\theta+3\cos^{8}\theta+\cos^{6}\theta$ equals
questions.explanation:
From $\sin\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$ one gets $\cos^{2}\theta=\sin\theta$. Then

$$
\cos^{12}\theta+3\cos^{10}\theta+3\cos^{8}\theta+\cos^{6}\theta=(\cos^{4}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)^{3}=(\sin^{2}\theta+\sin\theta)^{3}=1^{3}=1.
$$

questions.prompt: The range of $f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}+x+1}{x^{2}+x+2}$ ($x\in\mathbb{R}$) is
questions.explanation:
$$
f(x)=1-\dfrac{1}{x^{2}+x+2},\qquad x^{2}+x+2=\left(x+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac{7}{4}\ge\dfrac{7}{4}.
$$

Hence $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}+x+2}\in\left(0,\dfrac{4}{7}\right]$ and $f(x)\in\left[\dfrac{3}{7},1\right)$.

questions.prompt: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(x)+2f(1-x)=x^{2}$ for all $x$. Then $f(x)$ equals
questions.explanation:
Replace $x$ by $1-x$:

$$
f(1-x)+2f(x)=(1-x)^{2}.
$$

Together with $f(x)+2f(1-x)=x^{2}$, solve the linear system:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)+2f(1-x)&=x^{2},\\
2f(x)+f(1-x)&=(1-x)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Eliminating $f(1-x)$ yields $3f(x)=x^{2}-4x+2$, so

$$
f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4x+2}{3}.
$$

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}x}{x^{3}}$ equals
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{1-\cos x\cos 2x}{x^{2}}$ equals
questions.explanation:
$\cos x=1-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+O(x^{4})$ and $\cos 2x=1-2x^{2}+O(x^{4})$, so

$$
\cos x\cos 2x=1-\dfrac{5}{2}x^{2}+O(x^{4})\implies 1-\cos x\cos 2x=\dfrac{5}{2}x^{2}+O(x^{4}).
$$

The limit is $\dfrac{5}{2}$.

questions.prompt: Let $[\,\cdot\,]$ denote the greatest integer function. The number of points of discontinuity of $f(x)=[x^{2}]$ in the open interval $(-2,2)$ is
questions.explanation:
$[x^{2}]$ (greatest integer function) jumps wherever $x^{2}$ is a positive integer. In $(-2,2)$ one has $x^{2}\in\{1,2,3\}$ at

$$
x=\pm 1,\ \pm\sqrt{2},\ \pm\sqrt{3},
$$

six points in all.

questions.prompt: If $y=\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\sqrt{x+\cdots}}}$ ($x>0$), then $y'(2)$ equals
questions.explanation: $y^{2}=x+y$. Differentiating: $2yy'=1+y'$, so $y'=\dfrac{1}{2y-1}$. At $x=2$, $y^{2}-y-2=0$ and $y>0$ give $y=2$, hence $y'(2)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.prompt: If $x^{2}+xy+y^{2}=1$, then at the point $(0,1)$ the value of $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ equals
questions.explanation:
Differentiating $x^{2}+xy+y^{2}=1$ yields $y'=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}$. Differentiating again and simplifying,

$$
y''=-\dfrac{3y}{(x+2y)^{2}}.
$$

At $(0,1)$ one gets $y''=-\dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.prompt: If $x=t+\dfrac{1}{t}$ and $y=t-\dfrac{1}{t}$ ($t>1$), then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $t=2$ equals
The curves $y^{2}=4x$ and $x^{2}=4y$ intersect at $(4,4)$. If $\theta$ is the acute angle between their tangents there, then $\tan\theta$ equals
questions.explanation:
For $y^{2}=4x$, $m_{1}=\dfrac{2}{y}$; for $x^{2}=4y$, $m_{2}=\dfrac{x}{2}$. At $(4,4)$, $m_{1}=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $m_{2}=2$, so

$$
\tan\theta=\left\lvert\dfrac{2-1/2}{1+2\cdot(1/2)}\right\rvert=\dfrac{3}{4}.
$$

questions.prompt: The absolute minimum value of $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$ on $[-2,2]$ is
questions.explanation:
$f'(x)=3(x^{2}-1)=0$ at $x=\pm 1$. Evaluating,

$$
f(-2)=-2,\quad f(-1)=2,\quad f(1)=-2,\quad f(2)=2.
$$

The absolute minimum on $[-2,2]$ is $-2$.

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi / 4}\tan^{4}x\, dx$ equals
questions.explanation:
With $I_{n}=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tan^{n}x\, dx$ ($n>1$), one has $I_{n}+I_{n-2}=\dfrac{1}{n-1}$. Thus $I_{2}=1-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and

$$
I_{4}=\dfrac{1}{3}-I_{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{2}{3}.
$$

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi / 4}\sqrt{\tan x}\, dx$ equals
questions.explanation: The substitution $t=\sqrt{\tan x}$ reduces the integral to a standard rational form whose value on $[0,1]$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\, dx$ equals
questions.explanation:
Let $I$ be the given integral. The substitution $x\mapsto\pi-x$ yields

$$
2I=\pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^{2}x}\, dx=\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{du}{1+u^{2}}=\pi\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2},
$$

so $I=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{4}$.

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{dx}{(1+x)(1+x^{2})}$ equals
questions.explanation:
Partial fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{(1+x)(1+x^{2})}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{1+x}-\dfrac{x-1}{1+x^{2}}\right).
$$

Integrating from $0$ to $\infty$ gives $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi / 4}\ln(1+\tan x)\, dx$ equals
questions.explanation:
Let $I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan x)\, dx$. The substitution $x\mapsto\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x$ gives $\tan\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-x\right)=\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}$, so

$$
I=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln\!\left(1+\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}\right)\, dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln\!\left(\dfrac{2}{1+\tan x}\right)\, dx=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\ln 2-I.
$$

Hence $2I=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\ln 2$ and $I=\dfrac{\pi}{8}\ln 2$.

questions.prompt: The area of the region enclosed by $y=\lvert x\rvert$ and $y=2-x^{2}$ is
questions.explanation:
The curves meet at $x=\pm 1$. The enclosed area is

$$
2\int_{0}^{1}\bigl((2-x^{2})-x\bigr)\, dx=2\left[2x-\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}=\dfrac{7}{3}.
$$

questions.prompt: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}e^{\lfloor x\rfloor}\, dx$ equals
Let $y$ satisfy $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}y(t)\, dt$ with $y(0)=1$. Then $y(1)$ equals
questions.explanation:
Let $c=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}y(t)\, dt$. Then $y'+2y=c$, so $y=\dfrac{c}{2}+Ke^{-2x}$. The conditions $y(0)=1$ and $\int_{0}^{1}y=c$ give

$$
c=\dfrac{2(e^{2}-1)}{3e^{2}-1},\qquad y(1)=\dfrac{e^{2}+1}{3e^{2}-1}.
$$

questions.prompt: Let $A$ be a nonsingular $3\times 3$ matrix with $\lvert A\rvert=2$. Then $\operatorname{adj}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})\bigr)$ equals
questions.explanation:
For order $3$, $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj} M)=\lvert M\rvert M$. Taking $M=A^{-1}$ gives

$$
\operatorname{adj}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})\bigr)=\lvert A^{-1}\rvert\,A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\lvert A\rvert}A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{2}A^{-1}.
$$

(Alternatively: $\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})=\lvert A^{-1}\rvert A=\dfrac{1}{2}A$, and $\operatorname{adj}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}A\right)=\dfrac{1}{4}\operatorname{adj} A=\dfrac{1}{4}\lvert A\rvert A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{2}A^{-1}$.)

questions.prompt: If $A$ is a square matrix satisfying $A^{2}=I$, then $(A-I)^{5}+(A+I)^{5}$ equals
The number of $3\times 3$ diagonal matrices with every diagonal entry in $\{-1,0,1\}$ such that $A^{2}=I$ is
questions.explanation: A diagonal matrix with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$ satisfies $A^{2}=I$ if and only if every diagonal entry is $\pm 1$. There are $2^{3}=8$ such matrices.

questions.prompt: $\begin{vmatrix} 1+\sin^{2}x & \cos^{2}x & 4\sin 2x \\ \sin^{2}x & 1+\cos^{2}x & 4\sin 2x \\ \sin^{2}x & \cos^{2}x & 1+4\sin 2x \end{vmatrix}$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ equals
questions.explanation:
Perform $R_{1}\to R_{1}-R_{3}$ and $R_{2}\to R_{2}-R_{3}$:

$$
\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ \sin^{2}x & \cos^{2}x & 1+4\sin 2x \end{vmatrix}=1+4\sin 2x+\cos^{2}x+\sin^{2}x=2+4\sin 2x.
$$

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so the value is $2+2\sqrt{3}$.

questions.prompt: If $f(t)=\begin{vmatrix} t & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & t & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & t \end{vmatrix}$, then $f'(0)$ equals
Let $P=[p_{ij}]$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with $\lvert P\rvert=4$, and let $Q=[q_{ij}]$ where $q_{ij}=2^{i+j}p_{ij}$. Then $\lvert Q\rvert$ equals
questions.explanation: Factoring $2^{i}$ from row $i$ and $2^{j}$ from column $j$ multiplies the determinant by $2^{1+2+3}\cdot 2^{1+2+3}=2^{12}$. Hence $\lvert Q\rvert=2^{12}\lvert P\rvert=2^{14}$.

questions.prompt:
The system

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+y+z&=3,\\
x+2y+3z&=4,\\
x+4y+\lambda z&=5
\end{aligned}
$$

has a unique solution if and only if
questions.explanation:
The coefficient determinant is

$$
\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=\lambda-7.
$$

Unique solution $\iff\lambda\neq 7$.

questions.prompt:
The homogeneous system

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+y+z&=0,\\
2x+3y+z&=0,\\
3x+5y+\lambda z&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

has a nontrivial solution if and only if $\lambda$ equals
questions.explanation:
Nontrivial solutions exist precisely when the coefficient determinant vanishes:

$$
\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=\lambda-1=0\implies\lambda=1.
$$
